subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on cyber security threats and protection methods, then mark my answer against the CCEA spec.
promptWeak: Explain cyber security threats and protection methods for GCSE CCEA Computer Science simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which type of malware disguises itself as a legitimate or useful program to trick a user into installing it, but does not replicate itself?
questions.explain: A Trojan horse pretends to be a genuine program to trick the user into running it, then carries out a harmful action. Unlike a virus or worm, it does not replicate itself.

questions.q: How does a computer virus differ from a worm?
options: A worm needs a host file; a virus spreads on its own
There is no difference between them
A virus needs a host file and human action to spread; a worm self-replicates across networks without a host
A virus only affects hardware; a worm only affects software
questions.explain: A virus attaches to a host file and is activated when a human opens that file. A worm is self-replicating and spreads across networks on its own without needing a host file or human action.

questions.q: Which malware secretly records the keys a user presses to capture passwords and other sensitive data?
questions.explain: A keylogger is a form of spyware that records keystrokes to steal information such as usernames and passwords.

questions.q: What best describes a phishing attack?
options: Overloading a server with fake traffic
Sending fraudulent emails/messages that appear genuine to trick people into revealing sensitive information
Encrypting a victim's files and demanding payment
questions.explain: Phishing uses fake but convincing emails, messages or websites that imitate a trusted organisation to mislead people into sharing passwords, bank details or other sensitive data.

questions.q: An attacker phones an employee pretending to be from IT support and asks for their login password. What technique is being used?
questions.explain: Social engineering manipulates people psychologically (e.g. pretending to be trusted staff) to trick them into revealing confidential information or granting access.

questions.q: What is the main aim of a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack?
options: To secretly copy files from a computer
To overload a server with a flood of requests so it becomes unavailable to legitimate users
questions.explain: A DDoS attack uses many infected computers (a botnet) to flood a server with requests, overwhelming it so genuine users cannot access the service.

questions.q: A network of infected computers controlled remotely to carry out an attack is called a:
questions.explain: A botnet is a group of compromised computers ('bots') controlled by an attacker, often used together to launch a DDoS attack.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a firewall?
options: To monitor and filter incoming and outgoing network traffic, blocking unauthorised access
To scramble data so it cannot be read
questions.explain: A firewall sits between a network and external traffic, inspecting data packets and blocking those that do not meet its security rules, preventing unauthorised access.

questions.q: If sensitive data is stolen but was stored using strong encryption, why is the theft less damaging?
options: The data is scrambled and unreadable without the correct key, so it cannot be understood
Encryption deletes the data when copied
questions.explain: Encryption converts data into an unreadable form (ciphertext). Without the decryption key the stolen data is meaningless, so it stays confidential even if intercepted.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of two-factor authentication (2FA)?
options: Entering a password plus a one-time code sent to your phone
Using the same password on two websites
questions.explain: Two-factor authentication combines two different types of evidence, such as something you know (password) and something you have (a code on your phone), making accounts harder to compromise.

questions.q: A hospital gives nurses access to patient records but not to payroll, while accountants can see payroll but not medical notes. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Setting different levels of access (access rights) ensures each user can only reach the data they need for their role, reducing the risk of misuse.

questions.q: Why is keeping regular backups an important part of protecting data?
options: It allows data to be restored if it is lost, corrupted or held to ransom
questions.explain: Backups are copies of data stored separately. If the original is lost, corrupted, or encrypted by ransomware, the backup can be used to restore it.

questions.q: The Data Protection Act (2018) mainly governs:
options: The copying of software and media
How personal data must be collected, stored and used fairly and securely
questions.explain: The Data Protection Act sets out rules for handling personal data, including that it must be kept secure, accurate, used only for stated purposes and not kept longer than needed.

questions.q: A company keeps customers' personal details but never updates them, so many are out of date. Which Data Protection principle is being broken?
options: Data must be encrypted at all times
Data must be printed and stored on paper
Data must never be shared internally
Data must be kept accurate and up to date
questions.explain: A key Data Protection principle is that personal data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. Storing out-of-date details breaches this principle.

questions.q: Which action would be an offence under the Computer Misuse Act (1990)?
options: Downloading music you have paid for
Gaining unauthorised access to someone else's computer system
questions.explain: The Computer Misuse Act makes it illegal to gain unauthorised access to computer material, access it to commit further crimes, or make unauthorised modifications to data.

questions.q: A student guesses a teacher's password, logs into the school system and changes some grades. Which offences under the Computer Misuse Act apply?
options: Unauthorised access AND unauthorised modification of data
Neither, because they are a pupil
questions.explain: Logging in without permission is unauthorised access, and altering the grades is unauthorised modification of computer material - both are offences under the Computer Misuse Act.

questions.q: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (1988) is mainly designed to:
options: Set rules for recycling old computers
Protect the creators of original work from having it copied or used without permission
Control how personal data is stored
questions.explain: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act protects intellectual property such as software, music, images and text, making it illegal to copy or distribute them without the owner's permission.

questions.q: Which of the following is an environmental concern linked to digital technology?
options: Electronic waste (e-waste) from discarded devices and the energy used by data centres
questions.explain: Environmental impacts of digital technology include e-waste from disposed hardware and the large amounts of electricity used to power and cool devices and data centres.

questions.q: A firm replaces all its computers every year and sends the old ones straight to landfill. Which impacts does this raise?
options: Ethical and environmental - waste of resources and harmful e-waste
questions.explain: Frequent replacement and landfill disposal is both an ethical issue (wasteful use of resources) and an environmental one (toxic e-waste), rather than simply a technical or security matter.
